answer.answer_text: The provided evidence does not contain definitions or descriptions of the roles 'provider', 'importer', 'distributor', 'deployer', 'manufacturer', or other relevant regulated actors as defined under the EU AI Act. The evidence includes amendments to other regulations (e.g., due diligence statements, authorised representatives in other contexts, governance structures, and unrelated sectoral rules) but does not define or reference the specific economic operator roles under the EU AI Act. Therefore, it is not possible to determine which operators qualify for these roles or whether one entity can occupy more than one role under the AI Act.

The provided evidence does not contain sufficient information to determine whether an AI-enabled medical device qualifies as a high-risk AI system under the AI Act, or whether such classification follows from its intended purpose, status as a medical device or safety component, conformity-assessment requirements, or a combination thereof. While the evidence includes references to medical device directives (e.g., Council Directive 93/42/EEC), the AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689), and related concepts such as high-risk AI systems, conformity assessment procedures, and Annex III classifications, no specific AI-enabled medical device is described, nor is there any explicit linkage between a medical device's characteristics and the criteria for high-risk classification under the AI Act. The evidence lacks details on the device's intended purpose, risk level, or how it aligns with the specific use cases listed in Annex III of the AI Act that would trigger high-risk status.

answer.answer_text: Under the AI Act, non-EU manufacturers/providers of high-risk AI systems must ensure compliance with Section 2 requirements, implement a quality management system per Article 17, retain documentation per Article 18, maintain logs per Article 19, undergo conformity assessment per Article 43 before market placement, issue an EU declaration of conformity per Article 47, affix CE marking per Article 48, register per Article 49(1), take corrective actions and provide information per Article 20, demonstrate conformity upon request per Article 16(k), and ensure accessibility compliance per Directives (EU) 2016/2102 and (EU) 2019/882 per Article 16(l). EU importers must not place non-conforming or falsified high-risk AI systems on the market, inform providers, authorized representatives, and market surveillance authorities of risks per Article 23(1), indicate their contact details per Article 23(2), ensure storage/transport conditions do not jeopardize compliance per Article 23(3), retain copies of notified body certificates, instructions for use, and EU declarations of conformity for 10 years post-market placement per Article 23(4), provide documentation to competent authorities upon request per Article 23(5), and cooperate with authorities to mitigate risks per Article 23(6). Distributors must verify CE marking, EU declaration of conformity, and instructions for use before market availability per Article 24(1), withhold non-conforming systems until brought into conformity per Article 24(2), inform providers or importers of risks per Article 24(2), ensure storage/transport conditions maintain compliance per Article 24(3), retain documentation for 10 years per Article 24(4), provide information to authorities upon request per Article 24(5), and cooperate with authorities per Article 24(6). Healthcare organisation deployers must perform fundamental rights impact assessments before first use per Article 26(1), update assessments if elements change per Article 26(1), notify market surveillance authorities of assessment results per Article 26(2), and ensure assessments complement data protection impact assessments where applicable per Article 26(3).

claims.text: Non-EU manufacturers/providers must ensure that their high-risk AI systems are compliant with the requirements set out in Section 2.

Non-EU manufacturers/providers must indicate on the high-risk AI system or, where that is not possible, on its packaging or its accompanying documentation, as applicable, their name, registered trade name or registered trade mark, the address at which they can be contacted.
Non-EU manufacturers/providers must have a quality management system in place which complies with Article 17.
Non-EU manufacturers/providers must keep the documentation referred to in Article 18.
Non-EU manufacturers/providers must, when under their control, keep the logs automatically generated by their high-risk AI systems as referred to in Article 19.

Non-EU manufacturers/providers must ensure that the high-risk AI system undergoes the relevant conformity assessment procedure as referred to in Article 43, prior to its being placed on the market or put into service.
Non-EU manufacturers/providers must draw up an EU declaration of conformity in accordance with Article 47.

Non-EU manufacturers/providers must affix the CE marking to the high-risk AI system or, where that is not possible, on its packaging or its accompanying documentation, to indicate conformity with this Regulation, in accordance with Article 48.
Non-EU manufacturers/providers must comply with the registration obligations referred to in Article 49(1).
Non-EU manufacturers/providers must take the necessary corrective actions and provide information as required in Article 20.
Non-EU manufacturers/providers must, upon a reasoned request of a national competent authority, demonstrate the conformity of the high-risk AI system with the requirements set out in Section 2.
Non-EU manufacturers/providers must ensure that the high-risk AI system complies with accessibility requirements in accordance with Directives (EU) 2016/2102 and (EU) 2019/882.

EU importers must not place the system on the market until it has been brought into conformity where they have sufficient reason to consider that a high-risk AI system is not in conformity with this Regulation, or is falsified, or accompanied by falsified documentation.

EU importers must inform the provider of the system, the authorised representative and the market surveillance authorities to that effect where the high-risk AI system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1).

EU importers must indicate their name, registered trade name or registered trade mark, and the address at which they can be contacted on the high-risk AI system and on its packaging or its accompanying documentation, where applicable.

EU importers must ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise its compliance with the requirements set out in Section 2.

EU importers must keep, for a period of 10 years after the high-risk AI system has been placed on the market or put into service, a copy of the certificate issued by the notified body, where applicable, of the instructions for use, and of the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47.

EU importers must provide the relevant competent authorities, upon a reasoned request, with all the necessary information and documentation, including that referred to in paragraph 5, to demonstrate the conformity of a high-risk AI system with the requirements set out in Section 2 in a language which can be easily understood by them.

EU importers must cooperate with the relevant competent authorities in any action those authorities take in relation to a high-risk AI system placed on the market by the importers, in particular to reduce and mitigate the risks posed by it.

Distributors must verify that it bears the required CE marking, that it is accompanied by a copy of the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47 and instructions for use, and that the provider and the importer of that system, as applicable, have complied with their respective obligations as laid down in Article 16, points (b) and (c) and Article 23(3).

Distributors must not make the high-risk AI system available on the market until the system has been brought into conformity with those requirements where a distributor considers or has reason to consider, on the basis of the information in its possession, that a high-risk AI system is not in conformity with the requirements set out in Section 2.
Distributors must inform the provider or the importer of the system, as applicable, to that effect where the high-risk AI system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1).

Distributors must ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions, where applicable, do not jeopardise its compliance with the requirements set out in Section 2.

Distributors must keep, for a period of 10 years after the high-risk AI system has been placed on the market or put into service, a copy of the certificate issued by the notified body, where applicable, of the instructions for use, and of the EU declaration of conformity referred to in Article 47.

Distributors must provide the relevant competent authorities, upon a reasoned request, with all the necessary information and documentation, including that referred to in paragraph 5, to demonstrate the conformity of a high-risk AI system with the requirements set out in Section 2 in a language which can be easily understood by them.

Distributors must cooperate with the relevant competent authorities in any action those authorities take in relation to a high-risk AI system placed on the market by the distributors, in particular to reduce and mitigate the risks posed by it.
Healthcare organisation deployers must perform the fundamental rights impact assessment prior to the first use of the high-risk AI system.
Healthcare organisation deployers may, in similar cases, rely on previously conducted fundamental rights impact assessments or existing impact assessments carried out by provider.

Healthcare organisation deployers must take the necessary steps to update the information if, during the use of the high-risk AI system, the deployer considers that any of the elements listed in paragraph 1 has changed or is no longer up to date.

Healthcare organisation deployers must notify the market surveillance authority of its results, submitting the filled-out template referred to in paragraph 5 of this Article as part of the notification.
Healthcare organisation deployers may be exempt from the obligation to notify in the case referred to in Article 46(1).

Healthcare organisation deployers must ensure that the fundamental rights impact assessment referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article complements the data protection impact assessment conducted pursuant to Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 or Article 27 of Directive (EU) 2016/680 if any of the obligations laid down in this Article is already met through such assessment.

The evidence primarily concerns unrelated topics such as inland waterway authorities, Europol's data processing, asset recovery directives, Commission data handling, and UK GDPR provisions on automated decision-making, none of which directly address the interaction between the AI Act and GDPR in the specified contexts.

The provided evidence does not contain any information about the AI Act, GDPR, or their potential tensions, overlapping duties, or situations where compliance with one regime does not establish compliance with the other. The evidence is exclusively focused on topics such as skin irritation test methods, false negative rates in test methods, pharmaceutical market distinctions (OTC vs. prescription medicines), and medical device definitions under Council Directive 93/42/EEC. None of the evidence addresses artificial intelligence regulation, data protection law, or any intersection between the AI Act and GDPR.

presentation.overview: The retrieved evidence does not contain sufficient information to determine the economic operator roles under the EU AI Act, the high-risk classification of the AI-enabled medical device, the specific obligations of operators, conditions for provider role changes, AI Act-GDPR interactions, regulatory tensions, or post-deployment responsibilities for performance degradation. While some obligations for high-risk AI systems are partially supported in q003, they cannot be applied to this scenario without confirmation that the device qualifies as high-risk or that the actors fall within the defined roles. All major conclusions require evidence not present in the supplied materials.

sections.title: Economic Operator Roles under the EU AI Act
sections.answer_text: It cannot be determined which economic operators qualify as provider, importer, distributor, deployer, manufacturer, or manufacturer, nor whether one entity can occupy multiple roles, as the evidence does not contain definitions or descriptions of these roles under the EU AI Act.

sections.title: High-Risk AI System Classification
sections.answer_text: It cannot be determined whether the AI-enabled medical device qualifies as a high-risk AI system under the AI Act, or whether such classification follows from its intended purpose, status as a medical device or safety component, conformity-assessment requirements, or a combination thereof, as the evidence lacks specifics on the device’s intended purpose, risk level, or linkage to Annex III use cases.

sections.title: Obligations of Operators under the AI Act
sections.answer_text: While general obligations for non-EU manufacturers/providers, EU importers, distributors, and healthcare organisation deployers of high-risk AI systems are partially supported by evidence in q003, these cannot be applied to the scenario without confirmation that the device is high-risk and that the actors fall within the regulated roles defined by the AI Act.

assertion.subject: Source chunk L_202401689EN:chunk_57
assertion.object: What specific obligations apply to the non-EU manufacturer/provider, EU importer, distributor, and healthcare organisation deployer under the AI Act, distinguishing pre-market and post-deployment obligations?

sources.excerpt:
(a) ensure that their high-risk AI systems are compliant with the requirements set out in Section 2; (b) indicate on the high-risk AI system or, where that is not possible, on its packaging or its accompanying documentation, as applicable, their name, registered trade name or registered trade mark, the address at which they can be contacted; (c) have a quality management system in place which complies with Article 17; (d) keep the documentation referred to in Article 18; (e) when under their control, keep the logs automatically generated by their high-risk AI systems as referred to in Article 19; (f) ensure that the high-risk AI system undergoes the relevant conformity assessment procedure as referred to in Article 43, prior to its being placed on the market or put into service; (g) draw up an EU declaration of conformity in accordance with Article 47; (h) affix the CE marking to the high-risk AI system or, where that is not possible, on its packaging or its accompanying documentation, to indicate conformity with this Regulation, in accordance with Article 48; (i) comply with the registration obligations referred to in Article 49(1); (j) take the necessary corrective actions and provide information as required in Article 20; (k) upon a reasoned request of a national competent authority, demonstrate the conformity of the high-risk AI system with the requirements set out in Section 2; (l) ensure that the high-risk AI system complies with accessibility requirements in accordance with Directives (EU) 2016/2102 and (EU) 2019/882.
Article 17
Quality management system
1. Providers of high-risk AI systems shall put a quality management system in place that ensures compliance with this Regulation. That system shall be documented in a systematic and orderly manner in the form of written policies, procedures and instructions, and shall include at least the following aspects:
(a) a strategy for regulatory compliance, including compliance with conformity assessment procedures and procedures for the management of modifications to the high-risk AI system; (b) techniques, procedures and systematic actions to be used for the design, design control and design verification of the high-risk AI system; (c) techniques, procedures and systematic actions to be used for the development, quality control and quality assurance of the high-risk AI system; (d) examination, test and validation procedures to be carried out before, during and after the development of the high-risk AI system, and the frequency with which they have to be carried out; (e) technical specifications, including standards, to be applied and, where the relevant harmonised standards are not applied in full or do not cover all of the relevant requirements set out in Section 2, the means to be used to ensure that the high-risk AI system complies with those requirements; (f) systems and procedures for data management, including data acquisition, data collection, data analysis, data labelling, data storage, data filtration, data mining, data aggregation, data retention and any other operation regarding the data that is performed before and for the purpose of the placing on the market or the putting into service of high-risk AI systems; (g) the risk management system referred to in Article 9; (h) the setting-up, implementation and maintenance of a post-market monitoring system, in accordance with Article 72; (i) procedures related to the reporting of a serious incident in accordance with Article 73; (j) the handling of communication with national competent authorities, other relevant authorities, including those providing or supporting the access to data, notified bodies, other operators, customers or other interested parties; (k) systems and procedures for record-keeping of all relevant documentation and information; (l) resource management, including security-of-supply related measures; (m) an accountability framework setting out the responsibilities of the management and other staff with regard to all the aspects listed in this paragraph.

1. sections.title: Change of Provider Role due to Modifications
sections.answer_text: It cannot be determined under what conditions a substantial modification, retraining, fine-tuning, change in intended purpose, or post-market model update could cause another actor to become the 'provider' of the AI system, as the evidence contains no information on such conditions.

sections.title: AI Act and GDPR Interaction
sections.answer_text: It cannot be determined how AI Act obligations interact with GDPR regarding the processing of biometric and health data, including classification as personal/special-category data, lawful bases under Articles 6 and 9, purpose limitation, further processing for model improvement, automated decision-making obligations, or whether AI Act compliance supplies a GDPR lawful basis, as the evidence does not address this interaction.

sections.title: Tensions Between AI Act and GDPR
sections.answer_text: It cannot be determined whether there are apparent tensions, overlapping duties, or situations where compliance with one regime does not establish compliance with the other, as the evidence contains no information on the AI Act, GDPR, or their intersection.

sections.title: Post-Deployment Responsibilities for Performance Degradation
sections.answer_text: It cannot be determined what sequence of legal responsibilities would follow for the distributor, importer, provider/manufacturer, and deployer upon discovery of a material increase in false-negative rate for a patient subgroup, including monitoring, corrective action, notification, withdrawal/recall, or serious-incident obligations, as the evidence lacks specific provisions on such scenarios under the AI Act.
